items.ig_caption:
76.3%. That's how many simulated multi-stage cyber operations one AI model completed. 🤖

What The Hacker News and SecurityWeek reported (10 Nov):
→ Anthropic released Claude Fable 5.2 and Mythos 5.2, which share the same underlying model; Mythos ships with fewer guardrails
→ On Irregular's CyScenarioBench, which tests whether a model can plan and execute a multi-stage cyber operation in a realistic environment, Fable 5.2 completed 76.3% of challenges
→ Fable 5.1 scored 61.7% and OpenAI's GPT-6 Cyber 61%, as reported
→ Fable 5.2 classifiers stop penetration testing and exploit generation for general users; Mythos 5.2 is limited to vetted organizations
→ In Anthropic's sandbox test, Mythos 5.2 relied on credentials or files left outside the sandbox 3.1% of the time, down from 39% for Mythos 5

What it means for defenders: the time between a bug going public and someone being able to chain it into an attack keeps shrinking. Shorten patch deadlines for internet-facing systems and test your detections against multi-stage chains, not single alerts.

cover.hook: One flaw in an AI inference engine. 18 AI agents' chat history taken.
cover.sub: NEAR AI says an attacker exploited a remote code execution flaw in SGLang and moved further into its systems.

slides.title: What happened
slides.body: NEAR AI says an attacker exploited a remote code execution flaw in SGLang, the open-source inference engine, and ran code on one of its inference servers. No CVE or affected versions have been named yet.

slides.title: The TEE didn't help
slides.body: Confidential-mode requests run inside a TEE. NEAR AI says the TEE does not protect against a flaw in the software running inside it, and SGLang runs inside. The attacker could also have seen that day's requests on the server.

slides.label: AI agents on an older deployment outside the TEE: chat history, settings and logs taken
slides.note: Plus account details of about 100 Private Chat users. Per NEAR AI, via The Hacker News (10 Nov)

slides.title: The response
slides.body: NEAR AI revoked all sessions and admin credentials, replaced agent tokens, took Private Chat offline, deployed an SGLang fix and revoked two customers' API keys found in logs. It's unclear if the SGLang project has shipped a fix.

slides.title: Do this week
items: List where you run SGLang or other inference engines
Keep inference servers away from admin systems
Keep API keys and tokens out of agent logs
Watch SGLang for an official fix and patch fast

reel.hook: Over a dozen orgs. Via a vendor they'd left.

segments.say: Over a dozen companies. Data pulled through a vendor they had stopped using.
segments.show: Researchers say an attacker used leaked IAM credentials for an AWS account tied to Qubole, the big-data platform, to assume cross-account roles that customers had created for it.

segments.say: The roles were never removed. Nearly two weeks of access, secrets harvested, whole buckets downloaded.
segments.show: Sentra says the Qubole roles were still in place after customers stopped using Qubole. From 14 to 26 Oct the attacker enumerated resources, collected secrets and took S3 data.

segments.say: List every cross-account role. Delete the ones for vendors you've left.
segments.show: Wiz calls the activity opportunistic, not matching typical state-backed priorities. Source: SecurityWeek, 10 Nov.

items.x_text:
Qubole supply chain attack: leaked IAM credentials for a Qubole-linked AWS account let an attacker assume old cross-account roles and pull data from over a dozen organizations' AWS environments, 14-26 Oct, per Sentra and Wiz.

#SupplyChainAttack #CloudSecurity
items.ig_caption:
Over a dozen companies. Breached through a vendor they had stopped using. ☁️

What SecurityWeek reported (10 Nov), from Sentra and Wiz research:
→ An attacker got IAM credentials for an AWS account associated with Qubole, the big-data platform
→ With them, it assumed the cross-account roles customers had created for Qubole and reached their AWS environments
→ Sentra says the roles were still in place after customers stopped using Qubole: "The doors the attacker used were old ones."
→ From 14 to 26 Oct it enumerated resources, harvested secrets, tested them with TruffleHog and took S3 data, sometimes whole buckets
→ Wiz calls it opportunistic and says it doesn't match typical state-backed priorities. Victims aren't named

Do this week: list every cross-account IAM role in your AWS accounts, delete the ones for vendors you no longer use, require an External ID on the rest, and alert on role sessions you don't recognise.

cover.hook: A broken login check. Admin over your hypervisors. Exploited now.
cover.sub: Vates says attackers are exploiting an auth bypass in Xen Orchestra. Fixed in 6.9.1 and 6.10.0.

slides.title: The flaw
slides.body: Vates tracks it as VSA-2026-062 (no CVE yet). A flaw in how Xen Orchestra's REST API parses its login cookie lets an attacker sign in as the owner of an existing token, with admin rights.

slides.title: Why it's bad
slides.body: Per Vates, that leads to code execution on managed pools and full takeover of XCP-ng nodes as root. That's your whole virtualization layer, not one VM. Vates says a threat actor is actively exploiting it.

slides.label: fixed Xen Orchestra versions (xo-server 5.211.2 and 5.213.1)
slides.note: Per Vates VMS advisory, via The Hacker News (10 Nov)

slides.title: Signs to hunt
slides.body: Vates lists: a running VM named pivot2, VMs set with 'hvm_serial: file', and files /etc/cron.d/zz-ustar, /etc/cron.d/zz-ustar2, /.ustar5 and /.ustar6. Found any? Rotate all passwords and secrets.

slides.title: Do this today
items: Take Xen Orchestra off the internet
Block empty auth tokens at your WAF or reverse proxy
Hunt for the IOCs; rotate secrets if found

reel.hook: One git clone could run someone's code.

segments.say: Clone the wrong repo with its submodules, and it can run code on your machine.
segments.show: CVE-2026-111760: Git patched a flaw that can let a malicious repository run attacker code when it's cloned recursively with its submodules.

segments.say: A very long file path gets cut short, and can end up named dot git.
segments.show: An integer truncation in Git's index: an over-long path passes a length check but is written under a shorter name the attacker can set to .git. No in-the-wild exploitation reported.

segments.say: Update Git, and apps that bundle it. Until then, no recursive clones of repos you don't trust.
segments.show: Fixed: 2.56.1, 2.55.1, 2.54.1, 2.53.1, 2.52.1, 2.51.3, 2.50.2. GitHub.com is already fixed. Source: The Hacker News, 10 Nov.

items.x_text:
Git CVE-2026-111760: a malicious repository can run code on a machine that clones it recursively with submodules. Fixed in Git 2.56.1 and 2.50.2-2.55.1; update apps that bundle Git too. No exploitation reported.

#Git #CyberSecurity
items.ig_caption:
One git clone could run someone else's code on your machine. 💻

What The Hacker News reported (10 Nov):
→ Git patched CVE-2026-111760, a flaw that can let a malicious repository run attacker code when it's cloned recursively with its submodules
→ The cause: an integer truncation in Git's index. A very long path passes a length check but is written under a shorter name that can be set to .git
→ Fixed in Git 2.56.1, plus 2.55.1, 2.54.1, 2.53.1, 2.52.1, 2.51.3 and 2.50.2, along with five other Git CVEs
→ GitHub.com is fixed; GitHub Enterprise Server fixes are 3.19.15, 3.20.11, 3.21.9 and 3.22.4
→ No in-the-wild exploitation was reported

Do this week: update Git on dev machines and build servers, update apps that ship their own Git, and until then don't recursively clone repositories you don't trust.
